name: Roman chair / hyperextension bench

lead: A Roman chair supports your hips while you bend forward and raise your torso again. It trains the lower-back erectors, glutes and hamstrings, which people use to hold a more upright stance and build a fuller back and posterior chain.

The chain is loaded back extensions, then stronger spinal erectors and glutes, then better posture and muscle. It is common strength equipment; no trials were found that test it for posture or appearance.

paras: Users do bodyweight extensions, add a held plate for more load, or use the rear pad for sit-ups. It usually sits alongside deadlifts, rows and core work, and strength gains build over weeks of regular training.
Specific safety guidance is not given in the sources consulted and no injury-rate studies were found. People with back injuries usually check with a clinician or coach about loaded back extension.

angle.text: Roman chairs load the lower back, glutes and hamstrings, building the muscle that holds you upright and fills out the back. It is widely used strength equipment; appearance-specific research is limited.

lead: A Roman chair, also called a hyperextension bench or back extension bench, is a padded training bench that supports the hips or thighs while the user bends forward at the hips and raises the torso again. People use it to build the lower back, glutes and hamstrings, which contribute to a thicker back, a fuller posterior and a stronger-looking upright posture.[1]

In the main exercise, the hyperextension, the user lowers the upper body toward the floor from the hips and returns to a straight-back position. Bodyweight supplies resistance, and a held plate or dumbbell increases the load. Variants include Roman chair sit-ups for the abdominals and a single-leg version that loads the hamstrings.[1][2]

Researchers have measured muscle activation on the bench. In a trial of resistance-trained women, the 45-degree Roman chair back extension activated the gluteus maximus about as much as the Romanian deadlift and activated the biceps femoris more.[3] Other studies have looked at how well it trains the lumbar extensors specifically.[4][5][6]
infobox: Hyperextension, Roman chair sit-up, single-leg hamstring variant

paras: The apparatus supports the body during exercises, with pads on which the hips or torso rest while the user moves.[1] Wikipedia notes that the article on the equipment has no history section and does not explain the origin of the name.[1]

In hyperextensions the lower back is the primary target and the buttocks and hamstrings assist.[1] In Roman chair sit-ups the user lies with the hips supported on the pad and curls up with the abdominals; the hip flexors stabilise the pelvis and may become prime movers if it moves, and the exercise is described as an old-school way to strengthen core stabilisers.[1] The name 'Roman chair' is also applied to a wall sit and a squat-like movement that use no apparatus.[1]

Back extension equipment comes in two main bench designs distinguished by the angle at which the lower body is supported. A 45-degree bench holds the exerciser almost standing and allows extension through a partial range, while the 90-degree version, which Wikipedia notes is also called the Roman chair, places the body horizontally and permits a full range of motion [7]. Users fold their arms in front of the chest or place hands behind the head, and can hold a plate or dumbbell to the chest for extra load [7].

The exercise is also done with no equipment, lying prone on the floor and lifting arms, torso and legs, with gravity as resistance [7]. A related machine, the reverse hyperextension, is described as training the glutes and part of the hamstrings in addition to the spinal erectors, with a larger hip range of motion [7]. In anatomical terms the word hyperextension here simply means actively extending the spine from a flexed position and is distinct from the joint-injury meaning [7]. The erector spinae run along each side of the spine and consist of the spinalis, longissimus and iliocostalis muscles [7].

The erector spinae is a group of muscles and tendons running along each side of the spine from the sacrum and hips to the base of the skull, in three columns: iliocostalis, longissimus and spinalis [8]. The muscles extend the spine and, working with the gluteal muscles, help maintain a stable posture in standing and sitting; the abdominal rectus is their antagonist [8]. Wikipedia lists hyperextensions among the exercises used to strengthen the erector spinae, alongside deadlifts, good-mornings, squats, bridges and planks, and notes that care is needed to avoid lower-back injury when training the muscles directly [8].

This anatomy explains the bench's place in physique and posture routines: the erectors give the back its thickness on either side of the spine, while the glutes and hamstrings that assist in the hinge shape the lower body. In the hip-hinge, the lower back is the primary target and the glutes and hamstrings assist [1].

Wikipedia's hyperextension article describes a floor version with no equipment, in which a person lies face down and lifts the arms, upper torso and legs against gravity, as well as a version on a stability ball and diagonal floor variations [7]. On benches, arms may be folded across the chest or hands placed behind the head with the elbows out, and weight can be held to the chest for more load [7].

The reverse hyperextension machine is described as training the erector spinae, gluteus maximus and part of the biceps femoris, with a larger hip range of motion reported in a cited 2019 study [7]. A related single-leg Roman chair exercise has been compared with the Nordic hamstring curl and single-leg deadlift in a hamstring-forces study [2]. The Roman chair name is also used for a wall sit and a Roman chair squat that use no bench at all [1].

In a randomized crossover study of 15 resistance-trained women using a six-repetition-maximum load, the Romanian deadlift and the 45-degree Roman chair back extension activated the gluteus maximus 94 to 140 percent more than a seated machine back extension did. The Roman chair produced 71 to 174 percent higher biceps femoris activation than both other exercises, and erector spinae activation did not differ between the three.[3] The authors concluded that all three suit lower-back activation and that the Roman chair was best for overall lower-limb activation.[3]

A controlled study of 16 healthy volunteers and 18 people with chronic low back pain examined a Roman chair variant with hips flexed at 40 degrees, describing the exercise as popular for back muscle endurance while noting that it does not exclusively target the back muscles.[5] Setups with the pelvis stabilised differently change which muscles do the work.[4]

A biomechanics study of ten men compared the Nordic hamstring curl, a single-leg Roman chair exercise and a single-leg deadlift; peak hamstring forces were generally highest in the Nordic curl, while the authors suggested the Roman chair and deadlift may suit strength increases in the biceps femoris long head and semimembranosus.[2]

A 12-week randomized trial of 15 healthy volunteers had one group (n=9) train once weekly on a 45-degree Roman chair, one set of 8 to 20 repetitions to exhaustion with hand-held plates. Their peak isometric lumbar extension torque did not change significantly (224.0 to 240.3 N-m) compared with the non-training control group (175.6 to 178.2 N-m), even though their training load increased.[6]

A review in the British Journal of Sports Medicine found that bench and Roman chair trunk extensions, free-weight exercises and machines without pelvic restraint all activated the lumbar extensors during the exercise, but that training studies suggest they may be less effective at producing chronic lumbar-extensor adaptation than restrained machines.[4] The authors attributed this possibly to the compound nature of the movements, which lets hip extensors share the work.[4]

Other studies have used the bench as a research tool: a 24-person trial used a 45-degree Roman chair protocol with added load to induce delayed-onset muscle soreness in the paraspinal muscles as an experimental low back pain model,[9] and a 164-student school study used a parallel Roman chair dynamic back extension as one of five trunk-endurance tests after a six-week core routine.[10] No published trial has measured visible posture, glute size or appearance after Roman chair training.

A small MRI study scanned eight adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis and nine healthy volunteers before and after a symmetric Roman chair back exercise to map muscle perfusion patterns in the paraspinal muscles [11]. A 2019 study of 24 people used a loaded 45-degree Roman chair routine to produce delayed-onset muscle soreness for studying low back function [9].

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and lifting communities
paras: On T Nation, the bench appears mainly as accessory work in training logs: powerlifting-style logs list hyperextensions with added plates after squats and deadlifts, and general logs list Roman chair leg raises among abdominal work.[12][13] Few threads discuss it as a posture or appearance tool, so its place in forum culture is mostly as a routine component.

In T Nation logs, powerlifters list hyperextensions with bodyweight plus added plates as accessory work after squats and sumo deadlifts, and a different log lists Roman chair leg raises in an abdominal block [12][13]. The Wikipedia articles on the equipment carry no history section and do not explain the origin of the name, so its history is not well documented in encyclopedic sources [1][7].

Wikipedia's article on the Roman chair gives no specific safety guidance, and the hyperextension article carries no spinal-safety section; it advises beginners on the 90-degree bench to start with light loads [1][7]. The erector spinae article notes care is needed to avoid lower-back injury when training the muscles directly [8]. The bench has been used in research on people with chronic low back pain and on adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis, where it served as a controlled way to load the paraspinal muscles [5][11]. Decisions about loading and technique for people with back conditions are matters for clinicians and trainers.

lore.intro: On T Nation the Roman chair is rarely the subject of a thread; it turns up inside training logs as back, glute and hamstring accessory work.[12][13]

claims.claim: Hyperextensions build the glutes and hamstrings as well as the lower back
The Roman chair is an effective way to strengthen the lower back
Back extension work improves posture and the look of the upper back
The bench is a good way to train the glutes, not just the back.
The 45-degree bench and the horizontal bench give different training stimuli.
Reverse hyperextensions work the glutes and hamstrings more than the standard bench.
Back extension work is safe for people with back problems.

timeline.event: A randomized trial of 15 volunteers tests once-weekly 45-degree Roman chair training for lumbar extension strength [6].
A controlled study compares a 40-degree hip-flexed Roman chair exercise in 16 healthy people and 18 with chronic low back pain [5].
A review in the British Journal of Sports Medicine discusses the specificity of exercises for conditioning the lumbar extensors, including bench and Roman chair extensions [4].
A 164-student school trial uses a Roman chair back extension as one of five trunk-endurance tests after a six-week core routine [10].

A 24-person study uses a loaded 45-degree Roman chair routine to induce delayed-onset muscle soreness in the paraspinal muscles; an MRI study uses the chair to examine paraspinal perfusion in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis [9][11].
A randomized crossover trial in 15 resistance-trained women compares the 45-degree Roman chair back extension with the Romanian deadlift and a seated machine [3].
A biomechanics study of ten men compares hamstring forces in the Nordic curl, single-leg Roman chair exercise and single-leg deadlift [2].
